title: Critics Mocked His Giant Sea Slug, Yet It Proved Memories Physically Grow New Nerve Tips
description:
Behavioral & Circuit Analysis — Eric Kandel (1970–2000): How a Giant Sea Slug's 20,000 Neurons Proved Memories Physically Grow New Synapses, grounded in Vincent Castellucci, Harold Pinsker, Irving Kupfermann, Eric R. Kandel (1970) (Science). Empirical findings show that mammalian brains pack 86 billion tiny microscopic neurons, making it nearly impossible in the 1960s to find ONE single synapse storing ONE specific memory. Psychiatrist Eric Kandel made a bold bet that outraged mammalian physiologists: switch to the California sea hare Aplysia californica — which has just ~20,000 neurons, the largest nerve cells in the animal kingdom (up to 1 millimetre wide, visible to the naked eye!).

At the circuit level, this episode examines how somatosensory cortex, hippocampus, white matter coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that in *January 1970 (Science, three back-to-back papers!)*, Kandel, Pinsker, Kupfermann, and Castellucci mapped a crystal-clear reflex circuit: ~24 siphon sensory neurons wire directly onto ~6 gill motor neurons. Touch the siphon gently with a water jet, and the gill retracts defensively.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Vincent Castellucci, Harold Pinsker, Irving Kupfermann, Eric R. Kandel (1970). Neuronal Mechanisms of Habituation and Dishabituation of the Gill-Withdrawal Reflex in Aplysia. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.167.3926.1745
- Fleur L. Strand (1979). Neurophysiology Handbook of Physiology. Vol. I: Cellular Biology of Neurons. Section I: The Nervous System Steven Geiger Eric R. Kandel. BioScience. https://doi.org/10.2307/1307806
- Steve Carney, Eric R. Kandel (2005). Eric Kandel: A life in learning and memory. Drug Discovery Today. https://doi.org/10.1016/s1359-6446(04)03331-8
